desc:
An arithmetic expression is given in two arrays. nums holds the operands in order, and ops[i] is the operator between nums[i] and nums[i+1], coded as 0 = addition, 1 = subtraction, 2 = multiplication.

You may put parentheses anywhere you like, so that the operations are carried out in any order that is a valid nesting (ignore the usual rule that multiplication goes first). Return every distinct value the expression can have, sorted in increasing order.

Example: nums = [2,3,4,5], ops = [2,1,2] is the expression 2*3-4*5. The five ways to evaluate it give -34, -14, -10, -10 and 10, so the answer is [-34,-14,-10,10].
hints: Think about the operation that is carried out last. It splits the expression into a left part and a right part that are evaluated independently.
Choose the last operator position m. Every value of the left part combined with every value of the right part through ops[m] is a possible result.
The same sub-expression nums[i..j] is needed from many different splits, so cache its set of values (memoization). A set also removes duplicate values.
editorial: Define go(i, j) as the set of values that the operands nums[i..j] can reach. If i = j it is just that one operand. Otherwise try every operator position m in i..j-1 as the one applied last, and combine every value of go(i, m) with every value of go(m+1, j).

Without caching the same sub-ranges are solved again and again, and the number of parenthesizations is the Catalan number (1,430 for nine operands). Caching the value set per range keeps the work to the sum over ranges of the product of the sizes of the two sets, and sets collapse equal values. All values stay below 9<sup>9</sup> in absolute value, which fits in 32 bits.
time: O(Catalan(m)) combinations in the worst case
